title: What a lottery can and cannot tell us
bodyMd:
When a popular secondary school has more applicants than places, some education authorities fill the places by drawing lots. For researchers this is a rare gift. Because the draw decides who wins, winners and losers differ, on average, only in their luck, so any later difference in their outcomes can be attributed to the school rather than to the kind of family that chose to apply. Two economists, Liesl Varga and Tomás Ederra, studied the lotteries of three heavily oversubscribed schools in one large city and found that, five years after the draw, the winners scored no higher on the national leaving examination than the losers, who had gone on to other schools.

It is tempting to read this as proof that the three schools' celebrated results owe everything to their intake and nothing to their teaching. The inference is too quick. A lottery compares only the children who applied, and applicants to a sought-after school are not a cross-section of the city: they tend to come from families that are well informed, ambitious for their children and able to secure a good alternative if the draw goes against them. What the study measures, then, is the effect of a place at one of these schools on such children, relative to the schools they would otherwise have attended. For them, it appears, the choice made little difference. For a child from a family that would never have applied, a place might matter more, or less; on that the lottery is silent.

None of this diminishes the study. On the question it can answer, a lottery supplies some of the cleanest evidence available to the social sciences, precisely because no one chose who won. The error lies in carrying that answer over to questions the lottery was never designed to address, such as whether the same schools would achieve the same results if they admitted a different kind of pupil, or if they were enlarged.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph prose passage about using school admission lotteries as evidence of a school's effect on its pupils. There is no table, figure or mathematical notation. The passage describes a study by two fictional economists of the lotteries of three oversubscribed secondary schools, which found that five years after the draw the winners scored no higher on the national leaving examination than the losers.

provenance.notes: Original passage written for this item set about a general methodological subject, admission lotteries as natural experiments, in our own words. The economists, the city and the study are invented; no real study, author or published article is described, quoted or paraphrased. The passage is built around a scope argument: the study answers one question well, and the author carefully lists the neighbouring questions it cannot answer. The second paragraph opens with a tempting conclusion that the author rejects, and the third opens with a concession, so a reader who takes either opening sentence for the thesis is misled.
